params.question: A patient presents with recurring skin swellings. Which pair of features, when present together, is most diagnostic of urticarial wheals?

answers.text: Intense pruritus and each individual wheal resolving within 24 hours without leaving a mark

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The two hallmark features of urticarial wheals are intense pruritus and transience — each individual wheal resolves completely within 24 hours without a residual mark, even though the eruption as a whole may last days to weeks.

answers.text: Diffuse, non-pruritic swelling with predilection for the lips and eyelids

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes angioedema — the same mast-cell–driven process occurring in the deeper dermis and subcutis. Angioedema is characteristically less pruritic and longer-lasting than the superficial wheal.

answers.text: Burning pain and each lesion persisting for more than 48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Painful lesions that persist beyond 24 hours and leave bruise-like discolouration suggest urticarial vasculitis, not ordinary urticaria. A skin biopsy showing leucocytoclastic vasculitis would confirm that diagnosis.

answers.text: Pruritus with residual hyperpigmentation after each wheal resolves

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Urticarial wheals resolve completely without leaving a mark. Residual hyperpigmentation after a lesion resolves points to a different diagnosis, such as a fixed drug eruption.

overallFeedback.feedback: The two diagnostic features are intense pruritus and individual wheal transience — each wheal lasts less than 24 hours and resolves without leaving a mark. The narration calls transience 'the single most important fact' in the entire topic.
Exactly right. Intense itch and individual lesion transience (<24 hours, no residual mark) are the two features you must elicit in the history to confirm urticaria.

interactions.label: Histamine released from degranulating dermal mast cells acts on H1 receptors to

params.question: Histamine released from degranulating dermal mast cells acts on H1 receptors to produce the three cardinal features of a wheal. Which combination correctly identifies these three features?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Histamine on H1 receptors causes vasodilatation, not vasoconstriction; increased permeability, not decreased; and itch, not pain. The resulting triad is a red flare, a raised oedematous wheal, and pruritus.

answers.text: Vasodilatation (flare), increased vascular permeability (oedema), and cutaneous nerve stimulation (itch)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. H1-receptor activation on dermal vessels produces vasodilatation (the surrounding red flare), increased vascular permeability with plasma leaking into the superficial dermis (the raised oedematous wheal), and stimulation of sensory nerve endings (the characteristic itch).

answers.text: Vasodilatation (flare), collagen deposition (fibrosis), and sensory nerve stimulation (itch)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Collagen deposition and fibrosis are features of chronic scarring conditions, not of urticaria. The wheal is caused by transient dermal oedema from increased vascular permeability, not by structural tissue change.

Purpura results from blood vessel damage or platelet dysfunction and is not a feature of ordinary urticaria. If a wheal-like lesion leaves bruise-like purpura, urticarial vasculitis should be considered instead.

overallFeedback.feedback: Histamine acting on H1 receptors produces vasodilatation (red flare), increased vascular permeability (raised oedematous wheal), and cutaneous sensory nerve stimulation (itch). Understanding this triad is the key to understanding why H1-antihistamines are first-line therapy.
Well done. This mechanism — histamine on H1 receptors producing flare, oedema, and itch — is what makes H1-antihistamines the logical cornerstone of urticaria treatment.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old medical student with chronic spontaneous urticaria needs treatment

params.question: A 30-year-old medical student with chronic spontaneous urticaria needs treatment that will not impair her ability to attend classes. Which is the most appropriate first-line agent?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chlorpheniramine is a first-generation H1-antihistamine with significant sedating and anticholinergic effects. Current guidelines recommend against first-generation agents as first-line because they impair alertness, learning, and driving.

answers.text: Oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for one week

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Systemic corticosteroids are not first-line for chronic urticaria. Their significant adverse-effect profile with repeated use makes them suitable only for short rescue courses in severe acute flares, not for ongoing management.

Correct. A second-generation, non-sedating H1-antihistamine at the standard licensed dose is the recommended first-line treatment. Cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine, loratadine, and bilastine all control symptoms effectively without the sedation that impairs daily functioning.

Hydroxyzine is a first-generation, sedating antihistamine. Although sometimes used as a short-term adjunct at bedtime, it is not recommended as first-line monotherapy for chronic urticaria because of its sedating and anticholinergic effects.

overallFeedback.feedback: The recommended first-line treatment is a second-generation, non-sedating H1-antihistamine (cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine, loratadine, or bilastine) at the standard licensed dose — chosen specifically because it controls symptoms without the sedation and anticholinergic effects of older agents.

Correct. The guideline-based first step is a second-generation non-sedating H1-antihistamine at standard dose. If inadequate after 2–4 weeks, the dose may be up-titrated before considering add-on therapies.
